title: How Long After Drinking Can You Drive? Why No Chart Is Safe
excerpt: How long after drinking can you drive? Why no chart or calculator can tell you when you're safe, how legal limits work, morning-after risks, and the sober-up myths that don't work.
metaDescription: How long after drinking can you drive? Why no chart tells you when you're safe, how legal limits work, morning-after risks, and why coffee won't help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** if you have to ask how long to wait, the safe answer is not to drive tonight. Your body clears alcohol at a slow, steady pace that you can't speed up, and that pace varies a lot from person to person and night to night. No chart or calculator can tell you the moment you personally are safe or legal to drive. After a heavy night, you may still be over the legal limit the next morning. And being under the limit doesn't mean you're unaffected: impairment starts well before 0.08%.

**The quick rules:** Decide how you're getting home *before* the first drink. If you drank, plan on a ride, a designated driver, transit, or staying over. Coffee, cold showers, food, and sleep do not lower your blood alcohol. After a big night, plan a car-free morning. If a breathalyzer says you're over, believe it; if it says you're under, don't treat that as permission. When in doubt, don't drive.

> **This is not legal or medical advice.** Drink-driving laws differ by country, state, and license type, and only a proper test measures your actual blood alcohol. This guide explains why the wait is longer and less predictable than most people think. It is not a way to work out whether you're "safe" or "legal" on a given night. **If you're unsure, don't drive.** If someone who has been drinking is very confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, or has cold, pale or bluish skin, that can be alcohol poisoning: call 911 (or your local emergency number) and don't leave them alone. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) lists what to watch for.

## Why There's No Magic Number of Hours

People want a simple rule like "wait an hour per drink." It sounds tidy, but it hides a lot of variation, and it's often too optimistic. How long alcohol stays in your blood depends on how high your blood alcohol got and how fast your body brings it down. Both of those change from person to person and night to night.

### What pushes your blood alcohol up

Your peak **blood alcohol concentration (BAC)**, the percentage of your blood that is alcohol, depends on:

- **How much you drank.** Count standard drinks, not glasses. A large pour of wine or a strong craft beer can be two drinks in one glass.
- **How fast you drank.** Three drinks in an hour push your BAC much higher than three drinks spread over an evening.
- **Your body size.** A bigger body has more water to dilute the same amount of alcohol.
- **Your sex.** On average, women reach a higher BAC than men of the same weight from the same drinks, mainly because of differences in body water.
- **Food.** Eating before or while drinking slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which lowers the peak. It does not make the alcohol disappear.
- **Mixers and carbonation.** Fizzy drinks can speed up absorption for some people.

If you want the full background on what BAC measures and how it's tested, our guide on [what BAC is](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) covers it.

### What brings it down

Here's the part people don't like hearing. Once alcohol is in your blood, your liver breaks it down at a fairly fixed rate that you can't speed up. That rate is an average across many people, and your own rate on a given night can be slower than the average for reasons you can't feel: body size, sex, genetics, liver health, medicines, and what you ate all play a part.

The main enzyme doing this work, alcohol dehydrogenase, gets saturated at fairly low levels of drinking. That's why drinking more doesn't make your liver work proportionally faster. It just means a longer queue. Our explainer on [how alcohol is metabolized](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-is-metabolized) walks through the chemistry in plain words.

### Your BAC can still be rising after you stop

Alcohol keeps absorbing from your stomach and gut for a while after your last drink. Peak BAC usually arrives somewhere around 30 to 90 minutes after you stop, and later if you ate a big meal. So the moment you put the glass down and feel "fine" is often not your peak. Driving home straight after "one last drink" can mean driving at your highest level of the night.

## Why We Won't Give You a Number of Hours

Many sites offer charts of "hours per drink" or a formula you can plug your weight into. We've left them out on purpose, because they invite exactly the wrong decision: doing the math at midnight and deciding you're fine to drive.

- **The averages hide big differences.** Two people of the same weight can clear alcohol at noticeably different speeds, and the same person can vary from night to night.
- **People count drinks badly.** Heavy pours, strong craft beers, doubles, and drinks topped up by someone else all make the night's total higher than it feels.
- **Your BAC may still be rising.** Alcohol keeps absorbing for a while after your last drink, so any estimate based on "how I feel now" can be wrong in the dangerous direction.
- **Zero alcohol isn't the finish line.** Even once your blood alcohol reaches zero, a hangover and a short night can still slow your reactions and attention.
- **Feeling fine is the least reliable signal of all.** Alcohol impairs judgment first, including your judgment about how impaired you are.

BAC calculators can be useful for one thing: understanding why heavy drinking takes so long to clear. They can't account for your liver, your medications, what you ate, or how big your pours really were. Never use one to decide you're fine to drive. Our guide on [what BAC is](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) explains what blood alcohol measures and how it's tested, without turning it into a countdown clock.

## Legal Limits Are Lower Than Many People Think

The legal limit is the line where you're automatically guilty of drink-driving. It is not the line where impairment starts. In most places, police can also charge you below the limit if your driving shows you're impaired. Our guide to the [legal alcohol limit to drive](/never-hungover/legal-alcohol-limit-to-drive) covers the rules in more detail.

| Where / who | General legal BAC limit |
|---|---|
| Most US states, drivers 21+ | 0.08% |
| Utah | 0.05% |
| US commercial drivers (trucks, buses) | 0.04% |
| US drivers under 21 | "Zero tolerance": usually 0.00% to 0.02%, depending on the state |
| England, Wales and Northern Ireland | 80 mg per 100 ml of blood (equivalent to 0.08%) |
| Scotland | 50 mg per 100 ml of blood (0.05%) |
| Canada | 0.08% is the criminal limit; most provinces have penalties starting at 0.05% |
| Australia, Ireland, and much of Europe | Often 0.05% for fully licensed drivers, lower for new or professional drivers |

Laws change, and there are extra rules for learners, new drivers, and professional drivers in many places. Check your local rules rather than relying on any summary, including this one.

### Why the limit isn't the real target

US road-safety research summarized by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration describes measurable effects at levels many people would call "barely buzzed":

- **Around 0.02%:** some loss of judgment, a relaxed feeling, a decline in visual function, and a reduced ability to do two things at once.
- **Around 0.05%:** reduced coordination, a reduced ability to track moving objects, difficulty steering, and slower response to emergencies.
- **Around 0.08%:** poor muscle coordination, worse judgment and self-control, and trouble with concentration, information processing, and perception.

Driving is the definition of doing several things at once while tracking moving objects. That's why the honest goal isn't "under 0.08." It's "not drinking before driving."

## How Long After One Drink Can You Drive?

This is the most common version of the question, and it's where people take the biggest gamble because they feel fine.

A single standard drink puts a lot of adults somewhere around 0.02% to 0.04%. For a larger man who drinks it slowly with food, that's at the low end. For a smaller woman on an empty stomach, it's at the high end. In either case, it's not zero, and it's in the range where NHTSA's summary describes effects on judgment and divided attention.

Some honest points:

- **Your "one drink" may be two.** A 9% IPA in a pint glass or a generous restaurant pour of wine can easily be 1.5 to 2 standard drinks.
- **If you're in Utah, Scotland, or a country with a 0.05% limit**, a couple of strong drinks can put you near or over the legal line.
- **Under-21 drivers and commercial drivers** may be over their legal limit after a single drink.

If you want a rule you never have to think about: **if you're driving, don't drink.** There's no waiting time after "just one" that we can promise is safe for you, so the plan that never fails is to choose between drinking and driving before the night starts.

## How Long After a Night Out Can You Drive the Next Morning?

This is where good people get caught out. You got home safely in a taxi, slept for six hours, and now you need to drive to work or do the school run. It feels like the responsible part is over. It may not be.

### Sleep doesn't speed anything up

Your liver clears alcohol at the same slow pace whether you're awake or asleep. After a big night that ran late, a few hours of sleep may not be anywhere near enough for your blood alcohol to reach zero. Many people are surprised by how many "morning after" drink-driving arrests happen on the way to work.

### Plan the morning the night before

Rather than trying to work out in the morning whether you've cleared, decide in advance:

- **If you have to drive early, keep the night light, or don't drink.** That's the only version of the plan that doesn't depend on guesswork.
- **If you're going to drink heavily, make the next morning car-free.** Arrange a ride, take transit, swap the school run, or start later.
- **If you wake up and aren't sure, treat that as your answer.** Not sure means don't drive.

### Even at zero, a hangover affects your driving

A hangover is what happens *after* your blood alcohol has fallen back toward zero. Its symptoms, including fatigue, headache, poor concentration, and slower reactions, are exactly the ones that make driving harder. Simulator studies, including work from researchers at Utrecht University led by Joris Verster, have found that people driving with a hangover and no alcohol in their blood showed impairment in a range similar to mild intoxication. The research is limited, but the direction is consistent: a bad hangover is not a great state for highway driving.

If you're wondering how long the hangover part lasts, see our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last). Our guide on [driving hungover](/never-hungover/driving-hungover) covers the morning-after picture in more depth.

## Things That Don't Help You Sober Up Faster

There are many myths about clearing alcohol quickly. None of them lower your BAC in any useful way.

- **Coffee.** Caffeine can make you feel more awake, but it doesn't remove alcohol. It can actually make things worse by making you feel able to drive when you're not. Our page on [coffee for a hangover](/never-hungover/coffee-for-hangover) explains what it can and can't do.
- **Cold showers or fresh air.** These may wake you up for a few minutes. Your blood alcohol is unchanged.
- **Eating after drinking.** Food before or during drinking lowers your peak. Food afterwards does very little to the alcohol already in your blood.
- **Water.** Staying hydrated is good for how you feel. It does not meaningfully speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol.
- **Exercise or "sweating it out."** Only a tiny fraction of alcohol leaves through sweat and breath. Almost all of it is processed by your liver at its own pace.
- **Throwing up.** Vomiting may remove some alcohol still in your stomach, but anything already absorbed stays in your blood. Repeated vomiting while very drunk is a warning sign, not a strategy.
- **Gum, mints, and mouthwash.** These can mask the smell. They don't change your BAC, and alcohol-based mouthwash can even raise a breath reading briefly.

We go through the evidence on each of these in [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism) and [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up). The short version: time is the only thing that works.

## Can You Trust a Personal Breathalyzer?

Personal breathalyzers can be a useful reality check, especially the morning after. But there are real limits.

- **Accuracy varies.** Cheaper consumer devices, especially semiconductor-sensor models, can drift and read low. Fuel-cell devices tend to be more accurate, but they still need regular calibration.
- **Testing too soon gives false readings.** Alcohol in your mouth from a recent drink, a burp, or mouthwash can produce a falsely high reading. Police breath-testing procedures typically include a waiting period of about 15 to 20 minutes for this reason. Wait at least that long after your last drink before testing.
- **Your BAC may still be climbing.** A reading taken shortly after drinking may be lower than where you'll be in 30 minutes.
- **A "legal" reading isn't a safety reading.** A result under 0.08% still means alcohol is affecting you.

The safest way to use one: **if it says you're over, believe it.** If it says you're under after a night of drinking, don't treat that as permission to drive; if you have any doubt, don't drive. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays on your breath](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-on-your-breath) covers breath tests in more detail.

## Things That Make Driving After Drinking Even Riskier

Some situations stack extra impairment on top of alcohol, so the effects can be stronger and last longer than you'd expect.

- **Medications.** Sedating antihistamines (like diphenhydramine in many sleep aids), sleep medicines, anti-anxiety drugs, opioid painkillers, muscle relaxants, and some antidepressants add to alcohol's effect on reaction time and alertness. Check the label for "may cause drowsiness" or "avoid alcohol" warnings, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.
- **Cannabis.** Combining cannabis with alcohol impairs driving more than either alone.
- **Lack of sleep.** Being tired already slows reactions. Add even a little alcohol and the effect compounds.
- **Not eating.** Drinking on an empty stomach raises your peak and makes you feel the effects faster.
- **Being new to driving.** Less experienced drivers have less spare attention to lose, which is why many places set lower limits for them.

## Practical Ways to Not Face This Question

The easiest way to answer "how long after drinking can I drive?" is to set things up so you never have to.

1. **Decide before you go out.** Choose who's driving, or decide that nobody is, before the first drink.
2. **Have a backup.** Keep a rideshare app set up, save a taxi number, check transit times, or arrange to stay over.
3. **Plan for the morning too.** If you have an early drive, either keep the night light or arrange another way to get there.
4. **Count standard drinks, not glasses.** Big pours and strong beers add up faster than you think.
5. **Pace yourself and eat.** It won't make it safe to drive, but it lowers your peak and makes the next day easier.
6. **Make it easy for others.** If you're hosting, offer non-alcoholic options and a couch.

The financial side is worth a moment too. A drink-driving conviction typically brings fines, legal fees, license loss, and much higher insurance costs, which together can easily run into thousands of dollars, before you even count the risk to yourself and others. A ride home is almost always the cheapest option.

## What About Hangover Supplements Like DHM?

You'll see supplements marketed for "recovering faster" after drinking. It's important to be clear about what they can and can't do when it comes to driving.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, and human data is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol in people, makes you sober faster, or makes it safe to drive sooner. Nothing you take changes the basic math: your liver clears alcohol at its own pace.

Where some people find DHM useful is the morning after, as part of a routine aimed at feeling better, alongside sleep, water, and food. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Just treat it as a comfort tool for the day after, never as a reason to get behind the wheel.

For the habits with the best evidence for an easier next day, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Your body clears alcohol at a slow pace that nothing speeds up, and that pace varies from person to person. No chart can tell you when you personally are safe to drive.
- Impairment starts well below the legal limit. Being "under 0.08" is not the same as being safe.
- After a heavy night, you may still be over the limit the next morning, so plan a car-free morning.
- Coffee, showers, food, water, and sleep don't lower your BAC. Only time does.
- A breathalyzer can tell you you're over. It can't tell you it's safe.
- The simplest rule is the one that never fails: **if you're driving, don't drink; if you've been drinking, don't drive. When in doubt, don't.**

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How long after drinking can you drive?**

There's no number of hours we can honestly promise is safe for you. Your body clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace that nothing speeds up, but that pace varies a lot between people and nights, and people tend to underestimate how much they drank. After a heavy night you can still be over the limit the next morning, and being under the legal limit is not the same as being unimpaired. The safe answer is not to drive after drinking that day or night, and if you have to ask, find another way home.

**Can I drive after one drink?**

One standard drink puts many adults somewhere around 0.02% to 0.04% blood alcohol, which is under the 0.08% US limit but not zero. Research summarized by the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration links levels as low as 0.02% to some loss of judgment and a drop in the ability to do two things at once. Smaller people, people who drink quickly or on an empty stomach, and drivers in places with lower limits (Utah, Scotland, much of Europe) have much less margin. The cleanest rule is not to drive after drinking at all.

**Is it safe to drive the morning after drinking?**

Not always. If you drank heavily late at night, you can still be over the limit the next morning, because sleep does not speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol. Even once your blood alcohol reaches zero, hangover symptoms like fatigue, slow reactions, and poor concentration can affect driving. Simulator studies have found hangover driving impairment in a range comparable to mild intoxication. After a big night, plan a car-free morning, and if you're unsure, don't drive.

**Does coffee or a cold shower help you sober up to drive?**

No. Coffee, cold showers, exercise, fresh air, and eating do not lower your blood alcohol in any meaningful way. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, which is the dangerous part: you feel more able to drive while your blood alcohol and reaction time are unchanged. Only time brings your blood alcohol down.

**How long after 3 or 4 drinks can I drive?**

There is no single number that fits everyone, and we don't think a chart is a safe way to decide. Weight, sex, food, how fast you drank, and how big the pours really were all change how high your blood alcohol gets and how long it lasts, and you can't measure any of that from the inside. Three or four drinks can put some people over the limit for hours. The reliable answer is not to drive after drinking, and to arrange your ride home before you start.

**Can I use a personal breathalyzer to decide if I can drive?**

Use it as a warning sign, not a green light. Consumer breathalyzers vary in accuracy and can read low, especially cheaper models or ones that haven't been calibrated. Readings also jump around if you test within about 15 to 20 minutes of drinking, burping, or using mouthwash. If a device says you're over, believe it. If it says you're under but you drank recently, don't treat that as permission to drive.

**Does DHM help you sober up faster so you can drive?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers blood alcohol in people or makes it safe to drive sooner. Most DHM research comes from animal and lab studies on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Some people take it to feel better the next day, but it should never change your decision about driving.
